title: EBRD ReDEWeB studies reached many towns but few projects advanced
programme: Renewable District Energy in the Western Balkans (ReDEWeB)
problem: Western Balkan cities, where 97 per cent of district heat comes from fossil fuels, lacked the plans and studies needed to attract investment in renewable heat.
solution: From 2019 the EBRD, backed by Austria's Federal Ministry of Finance, funded district heating decarbonisation plans and feasibility studies and worked on regulatory frameworks for investors.
funding: A EUR 4 million regional technical assistance programme backed by the Austrian Federal Ministry of Finance.
results: It worked with 11 cities in Serbia, four in Bosnia and Herzegovina and one each in Albania and Montenegro, but only a select few municipalities made progress. Bankwatch calls the regional dynamic not satisfactory.
serbia_reason: Most participating cities are Serbian, so the slow conversion of studies into investments directly affects Serbian heat utilities.
adapt_needed: Fund project preparation through to a bankable investment, and bundle small towns' projects, rather than stopping at feasibility studies.
blockers: Small towns' weak finances, limited technical capacity and complex financing schemes.
quote: Despite the provision of funding across the Western Balkans for numerous feasibility studies through the ReDEWeB programme, progress has been made by only a select few of the municipalities.

title: EBRD sovereign loan funds renewable district heating in 11 Serbian towns
problem: Serbian district heating companies run mostly on fossil fuels and lack capital to add renewable heat sources.
solution: An EBRD sovereign loan to the Republic of Serbia, topped up with Swiss and EU grants, finances small and medium projects (EUR 1–9 million) in district heating companies using geothermal, solar thermal, biogas, biomass and waste heat.
implementer: Government of Serbia with municipal district heating companies
funding: EBRD sovereign loan of up to EUR 30 million, plus a EUR 8.5 million Swiss grant and a EUR 3 million EU grant.
results: The project covers 11 Serbian cities and municipalities over four years, with expected lower energy costs and better energy security. Bankwatch notes many small Serbian towns need smaller EUR 1–3 million investments and face economic, knowledge and administrative burdens.
serbia_reason: This is Serbia's main development-bank financing line for renewable district heating. Its design and pace show what Serbian heat utilities can realistically absorb.
adapt_needed: Group small towns' projects so they reach a bankable size and add dedicated project preparation support.
blockers: Limited debt capacity of small municipalities and slow project preparation.
quote: Additionally, the Renewable District Energy (ReDE) project, which consists of a sovereign loan of up to EUR 30 million to the Republic of Serbia to finance investments in several district heating companies, involves 11 cities and municipalities in Serbia.

title: Pristina secures EUR 54 million grant for solar district heating
problem: Pristina needed a renewable heat source to expand its district heating network.
solution: A 58,000 m2 solar collector field with 410,000 m3 of seasonal heat storage and an absorption heat pump, plus an extension of the district heating network by 2028.
implementer: Government of Kosovo and Pristina municipality
funding: A EUR 54 million grant from the WBIF and KfW, with an EBRD loan agreement signed in 2022.
results: Grant and loan financing were secured in 2022, making Pristina one of the few ReDEWeB cities to reach a contract; the network extension is due by 2028.
serbia_reason: Serbian heat utilities can tap the same WBIF and KfW channels for large solar thermal with seasonal storage. It shows a non-biomass renewable option for a Western Balkan capital's heat network.
adapt_needed: Find land near the network for collectors and storage and size the plant to local heat demand.
blockers: Land availability near cities and high upfront capital cost.
quote: In 2022, Kosovo received a grant of EUR 54 million from the WBIF and KfW to finance the construction of the Big Solar Pristina project.

title: Sarajevo Canton approves EUR 50 million wastewater heat pump district heating
programme: Sarajevo Canton district heating heat pump project
problem: Sarajevo's district heating needed a low-carbon heat source.
solution: The cantonal government approved two 38 MW industrial heat pumps using wastewater heat, developed in partnership with the EBRD, with a WBIF grant application in preparation.
funding: A EUR 50 million project developed with the EBRD; a EUR 15 million WBIF grant application for capital costs is in preparation.
results: Approved in 2023; the feasibility study is complete, phase 1 funds are secured and the loan agreement was planned for 2024.
serbia_reason: Serbian towns such as Vršac and Kruševac have similar wastewater heat pump projects in the EBRD ReDEWeB pipeline. Sarajevo shows how a city can move such a project to approval.
adapt_needed: Map wastewater and other waste heat sources near each Serbian network and match heat pump size to them.
blockers: High upfront capital cost and electricity price exposure for large heat pumps.
quote: In 2023, the Government of the Sarajevo Canton in Bosnia and Herzegovina approved a capital district heating project of EUR 50 million.

title: Vienna bans fossil heating in new buildings through heat zoning
programme: Vienna climate protection areas and heat zoning plan
problem: New buildings kept locking in fossil gas heating for decades.
solution: Vienna bans fossil gas heating in new buildings in designated 'climate protection areas' backed by a heat zoning plan, and mandates and subsidises solar systems on new residential buildings.
results: Four districts already ban fossil fuel heating in new buildings, and a city-wide ban in all buildings is targeted for 2040.
serbia_reason: Serbian cities with large heat networks could use zoning to steer new buildings to district heating or heat pumps instead of individual gas boilers.
adapt_needed: Adopt heat zoning in municipal spatial plans and align it with district heating expansion plans.
blockers: No national legal basis for municipal fossil heating bans and strong reliance on gas.
quote: Vienna has a fossil gas ban as a heating solution in new buildings of the so-called ‘climate protection areas’, and the city has an aggressive heat zoning plan for them, with four districts already banning fossil fuel heating in new buildings and a targeted ban on fossil fuel heating in all buildings city-wide by 2040.

title: Danish EnergyLab Nordhavn pilot uses district heat pumps to balance grid
problem: A power system with more variable renewables needs flexible resources to stay balanced.
solution: The pilot used heat pumps in district heating to provide reserves to the power system by regulating their electricity consumption.
results: It demonstrated technical and economic feasibility, and research found district heating profit could rise by around 2.23 per cent by selling flexibility in energy and reserve markets.
serbia_reason: As Serbia adds wind and solar, heat pumps in municipal heat networks could help balance the grid.
adapt_needed: Open balancing and reserve markets to district heating operators with heat pumps.
blockers: Few large heat pumps in Serbian networks and limited access for small players to balancing markets.
quote: The pilot project EnergyLab Norhavn in Denmark has demonstrated the technical and economic feasibility of using the flexibility from heat pumps
